Setup guide

Start with the dry-run backend. You can inspect the configuration, exercise the tendon mapping, and connect a sensor adapter before connecting actuators.

Clone the OpenTDCR repository and open a terminal in its directory. Requires Python 3.10 or newer.

python3 -m venv .venv
source .venv/bin/activate
python -m pip install -e .
tdcr inspect --config configs/three_segment.example.json
tdcr teleop --config configs/three_segment.example.json --commands '1 w w 2 a q'

On Windows, activate with .venv\Scripts\activate. These commands never open a motor connection.

Try keyboard teleoperation

tdcr teleop --config configs/three_segment.example.json

Type a command, then press Enter. Select a segment with 1, 2, or 3; use w/a/s/d for a bounded bending step; type home to request the session reference or q to exit. This command-step interface makes each input explicit.

Robot geometry, servo IDs, winding signs, and limits live in configuration. The included nine-tendon configuration is an example, not a calibrated description of the supplied assembly.

Use a wired DualSense

python -m pip install -e '.[gamepad]'
tdcr teleop --config configs/three_segment.example.json --input dualsense

The optional controller path uses a standard DualSense over USB. Start with L1 released, then hold L1 and move the left stick for bounded steps. D-pad up/down selects a segment; Circle exits. Releasing L1 during a monitored move or losing fresh reports ends the session and requests torque-off. Bluetooth and DualSense Edge are not supported; real-controller validation is still pending.

Understand the hardware

The supplied STEP file describes the actuation module and mounts. It contains 16 modeled servo housings, which does not establish the number of bending tendons or their assignment. The long flexible backbone is absent from this assembly.

The historical assembly images show an earlier robot and are labeled as references. Confirm part revisions, missing printable parts, backbone design, and the wiring map before building. The release notes list the remaining verification work.

Bring your own measurement sensor

A sensor adapter implements read() and close(). Each read returns a measured position in millimetres, transformed into your documented robot base frame, together with the acquisition time on the host monotonic clock.

from opentdcr.sensors import PositionMeasurement

# Inside your adapter's read() method:
return PositionMeasurement(
    position_mm=(x_mm, y_mm, z_mm),
    timestamp_s=acquisition_time_on_host_monotonic_clock,
    frame="robot_base",
    valid=True,
)

Keep the timestamp of the original observation when returning a cached sample. Lost tracking should produce an invalid sample or raise an exception. Vendor reads must have a finite timeout.

# Exercise the supplied synthetic example, with no motor access.
python -m opentdcr sensor --sensor examples.sensor_adapter:create_sensor --samples 5

# Use your own importable adapter in a dry run.
tdcr teleop --config configs/three_segment.example.json \
  --sensor my_lab.sensor:create_sensor

The optional sensor gate checks measurement availability and freshness. It does not implement closed-loop position control. The separate calibration command uses measured tip movement to establish tendon references. Mechanical pretension, encoder reference, sensor transforms, and model identification are separate procedures; see docs/measurements.md.

Try sensor-independent calibration

tdcr calibrate --config configs/three_segment.example.json \
  --calibration-config configs/calibration.example.json

This default run uses synthetic measurements and never connects motors. The sequence loosens each tendon, detects a configured tip-motion threshold, applies a countback, and captures the final reference. For your own sensor, optional Lyra setup, local reports, and same-session teleoperation, see docs/calibration.md. This module acknowledges Lee et al., ICRA 2025.

Connect physical hardware deliberately

The current backend targets XL430-W250 servos and checks the model and bus configuration before enabling torque. Read docs/getting-started.md for register prerequisites, then create a measured, reviewed local configuration and establish the physical reference.

python -m pip install -e '.[hardware]'
tdcr inspect --config local.robot.json
tdcr teleop --config local.robot.json --hardware \
  --port /dev/ttyUSB0 --confirm-home

Use your machine’s actual port. The physical path requires an interactive terminal and explicit configuration review. --confirm-home records the current manually prepared posture; it does not perform homing or tension calibration. Keep a physical power cutoff available. This new driver still requires validation on the real robot.

Extend the stack

The archive includes AGENTS.md, a small API map, contributor guidance, regression tests, and a programmatic dry-run example. Start with src/opentdcr/; hardware access is isolated in the transport module.

python -m unittest discover -s tests -v
python examples/programmatic_dry_run.py

The lab’s experimental scripts, sensor recordings, calibration transforms, and internal Git history are excluded from this release tree.
